title: Payment connection pool timeouts
executive_summary: INC-012 (SEV2) affected payment-service between 10:10Z and the investigation window, with elevated API latency and errors and log entries reporting connection pool timeouts. Final status is ROOT_CAUSE_IDENTIFIED. The leading hypothesis (H1, confidence 0.95) is a configuration regression: change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04:00Z (cfg-56d39584). Baseline pool use (roughly 17 connections) now exceeds the cap of 10, so requests queue and time out. Pool-acquire timeouts began at 10:06:13Z with active=10 idle=0 and a growing waiting queue (logpat-payment-service-7d1739af). Timeout rate rose from a baseline of 0.1 to a window mean of 6.3 and error rate from 0.8 to 9.17, both with onset at 10:06 (met-payment-service-timeout_rate-0940-1035, met-payment-service-error_rate-0940-1035). Pool utilization rose from 34.95 to 69.43 with onset at 10:05 (met-payment-service-db_conn_util_pct-0940-1035). Request rate was flat (300 vs 299 rps), so load did not change (met-payment-service-request_rate-0940-1035). The critic approved this finding. The explanation is the most probable cause, not a confirmed fact. Two items remain unverified: the intent of OPS-2669 and whether restoring 50 clears the saturation.

hypotheses.description: Config change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04Z, so the pool saturates under unchanged load, causing pool-acquire timeouts and errors. Mechanism: db.pool.max_size 50->10 at 10:04Z -> pool capacity drops ~5x while request rate stays ~300 rps and baseline pool use (~35% of 50, roughly 17 connections) now exceeds 10 -> requests queue (waiting up to ~92), active=10 idle=0 -> 5s acquire timeouts -> timeout_rate ~0.1%->~11-13% and error_rate ~0.8%->~17% from 10:06 -> payment API errors. Postgres connection count falling ~23% is consistent with payment-service now holding fewer connections (cap of 10), not contradictory.
confidence_explanation: +0.08 proposed cause (10:04) precedes/coincides with first observed anomaly (10:05)

critic_review.summary: H1 is well supported and consistent in time. Config change cfg-56d39584 (db.pool.max_size 50->10, OPS-2669) is the only change in the window, and the payment-service log confirms the reload to max_size=10 at 10:04:00Z. Pool-acquire timeouts appear from 10:06:13Z with active=10 idle=0 and a growing waiting queue, meaning the pool is exactly at its new cap. Timeout and error rates move at 10:06, after the reload. Request rate is flat (300 vs 299 rps), so load did not change. Postgres latency is flat and Postgres connection usage fell, which fits an application-side cap rather than a database slowdown. Caveat: the rollback test (restore 50 and check recovery) and the OPS-2669 intent are not yet confirmed. These do not block approval. H2, H3 and H4 are rejected, as detailed below.

assessments.reasoning: Config reload to max_size=10 is confirmed in payment-service logs at 10:04:00Z. Pool timeouts start at 10:06:13Z with active=10, idle=0, waiting up to 78, which matches a pool saturated at the new cap. Timeout and error rate onsets follow. Load is flat and Postgres p99 is flat, which rules out a load or DB-slowness cause. The rollback test is still a useful confirmation but is not required for approval.

report_rollup() slow statements started at 10:01, but payment pool utilisation was at baseline (~35%) until 10:05, and no pool errors appeared until 10:06, after the config reload at 10:04. Postgres p99, CPU and connection usage show no lock or IO pressure, and Postgres connections fell rather than rose. The rollup is at most a background factor and does not explain the saturation timing. Caller identity is also unknown.
Payment request rate is flat (300 vs 299 rps) and upstream api-gateway rate is flat. No surge or retry amplification is evident. The pre-check already flags no valid supporting evidence.

Redis p99 (3.0 vs 2.99 ms) and cache hit rate are flat. The only support is a topology edge added 2026-09-15, which is structural and not an anomaly. No redis log or timeout evidence exists. The cited evidence is not a symptom of degradation.

alternative_explanations: Report_rollup() lock or connection holds in Postgres contributing to pool pressure (H2). Not supported by timing or DB metrics, but not fully excluded without pg_stat_activity data.
Traffic surge (H3): contradicted by flat request rates.
Redis degradation (H4): contradicted by flat redis latency and hit rate.

probable_root_cause.description: Config change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04Z, so the pool saturates under unchanged load, causing pool-acquire timeouts and errors.
probable_root_cause.label: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence)

root_cause_statement: ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED (critic-approved; still an INFERENCE from evidence): configuration_regression in payment-service - Config change cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) reduced payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 at 10:04Z, so the pool saturates under unchanged load, causing pool-acquire timeouts and errors.
corrective_actions: Restore payment-service db.pool.max_size to 50 (the pre-change value) as the immediate mitigation, after confirming the intended value with the OPS-2669 owner (cfg-56d39584).
Verify recovery after the rollback: confirm the waiting queue drains, timeout_rate and error_rate return toward baseline (~0.1% and ~0.8%), and db_conn_util_pct stabilizes.
Record the rollback test result in the incident timeline so the hypothesis is confirmed or refuted by outcome rather than inference alone.
If rollback does not clear saturation, collect pg_stat_activity and pool metrics to test the unexcluded alternative of report_rollup() holding connections (H2).
preventive_actions: Require review and a staged rollout for changes to database pool settings, including a documented expected value and a check of current pool demand against the new cap.
Add config-change validation that compares proposed db.pool.max_size against observed peak connection demand and rejects values that would saturate the pool at current traffic.
Tie every config change to its ticket (OPS-2669) with a stated intent, so that unintended values can be detected in review.
Review the earlier pool-exhaustion incident from last year to determine whether the same class of config-driven cause was missed and whether the runbook should check config changes first.
monitoring_recommendations: Alert when payment-service db_conn_util_pct stays above 80% for 5 minutes or when the pool waiting count is greater than 0 for more than 1 minute.
Alert on any payment-service timeout log matching 'Timeout acquiring connection from pool payment-db-pool' and on timeout_rate above 1% for 5 minutes.
Emit an event or alert on every config reload that changes db.pool.* values, including old value, new value, and change ticket.
Track pool active and idle counts and waiting queue length as dashboard metrics, and keep Postgres report_rollup() duration (logpat-postgres-44883ca5) under alert as a secondary signal.
limitations: The rollback test (restoring 50 and observing recovery) has not yet been performed, so the causal link is inferred from timing and metrics rather than confirmed by outcome.
The intent behind OPS-2669 (whether 10 was the intended value) has not been confirmed.

Without pg_stat_activity data, the possibility that report_rollup() lock or connection holds contributed to pool pressure (H2) is not fully excluded, though timing and database metrics do not support it.
Redis and auth-service metrics were used to reject H4; the analysis covers only the metrics available in the investigation window.
Confidence values are rule-based evidence-strength scores, not calibrated probabilities.
Investigation terminated because: critic verdict APPROVED
conclusion: The most probable root cause of INC-012 is configuration regression: the reduction of payment-service db.pool.max_size from 50 to 10 under cfg-56d39584 (OPS-2669) at 10:04Z. Under unchanged request load (about 300 rps), the pool cannot serve baseline demand, which produces acquire timeouts and elevated errors from 10:06Z. Traffic surge, Redis degradation, and Postgres-side saturation were rejected on the evidence (H2, H3, H4). The rollback test and confirmation of intent for OPS-2669 remain outstanding and should be completed to fully close the investigation.
